summary: Defines IMAP4rev1, which lets a mail client access and manipulate electronic mail messages stored on a server. It was replaced by RFC 3501.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP4rev1 lets a mail client work with the mailboxes on a mail server. The client sends commands to list folders, read or search messages, and set flags on them, and the server answers with the data and a result for each command. It has since been replaced by RFC 3501.

questions: what are the imap connection states
subtitle: The protocol a mail client uses to read and change the mailboxes stored on a mail server.

tldr.problem: A mail client needs a way to list the folders on a server, read and search messages inside them, and mark or move those messages, without downloading and re-uploading the whole mailbox.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP4rev1 is a line based command and response protocol over TCP, where the client names each command with a tag and the server answers with untagged data plus a tagged OK, NO or BAD result. Messages can be named by a permanent unique identifier or by their position in the mailbox, and only the parts the client asks for are sent.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2060 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 3501.

today: RFC 2060 was a Proposed Standard published in December 1996 and it replaced RFC 1730. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 3501.

sections.title: What IMAP4rev1 Does
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 lets a client access and manipulate electronic mail messages stored on a server. It permits manipulation of remote message folders, called mailboxes, in a way that is functionally equivalent to local mailboxes, and it gives an offline client the capability to resynchronize with the server. The protocol also covers creating, deleting and renaming mailboxes, checking for new messages, permanently removing messages, setting and clearing flags, parsing RFC 822 and MIME, searching, and selectively fetching message attributes, texts and portions of them. It does not specify a means of posting mail; that is left to a mail transfer protocol such as SMTP.

The protocol assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP, and an IMAP4rev1 server listens on port 143. A connection consists of establishing the network connection, an initial greeting from the server, and then a series of client and server interactions. Each interaction is a client command, then server data, then a server completion result response. All lines end with CRLF.

Every client command begins with a tag, a short identifier such as A0001 that the client generates afresh for each command. The server's completion response carries the same tag, so the client can match a reply to the command that caused it even when several commands are in progress at once. There are three completion responses: OK for success, NO for failure, and BAD for a protocol error such as an unrecognized command or a syntax error. Server data that is not a completion response is prefixed with the character *, and a server that needs more input sends a command continuation request prefixed with +.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP4rev1 is how a mail client talks to a mail server. The client sends one command at a time, tagged so it can match the answer, and the server sends back data and a result line saying whether the command worked.

sections.title: The Four Server States
sections.content:
An IMAP4rev1 server is in one of four states, and most commands are valid in only some of them. It is a protocol error for the client to attempt a command in an inappropriate state, and the server responds with BAD or NO, depending on the implementation.

The non-authenticated state is entered when a connection starts, unless the connection has been pre-authenticated. In this state the client must supply authentication credentials before most commands are permitted. The authenticated state is entered when a pre-authenticated connection starts, when acceptable credentials have been given, or after an error in selecting a mailbox; here the client must select a mailbox before commands that affect messages are permitted. The selected state is entered when a mailbox has been successfully selected. The logout state is entered when a client asks to log out, when the server shuts down, or when the connection is closed, and the server then closes the connection.

A successful LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE moves the connection from non-authenticated to authenticated, and a successful SELECT or EXAMINE moves it from authenticated to selected. A CLOSE command, or a failed SELECT or EXAMINE, returns it to the authenticated state. A rejected connection is closed at the start with a BYE greeting.
sections.plainLanguage: The server moves through four states: waiting for a login, logged in, reading a mailbox, and closing the connection. Each command is only allowed in some of them, so the client has to log in and select a mailbox first.

sections.title: How Messages Are Named and Marked
sections.content:
Each message carries attributes besides its text, and a client can retrieve them individually or together. Messages are accessed by one of two numbers: the unique identifier and the message sequence number.

A unique identifier is a 32-bit value assigned to each message which, combined with the unique identifier validity value of the mailbox, forms a 64-bit value that is permanently guaranteed never to refer to any other message in that mailbox. Unique identifiers are assigned in strictly ascending order as messages are added, they are not necessarily contiguous, and they persist across sessions. That persistence is what lets an offline client resynchronize its state with the server. The validity value is sent in a UIDVALIDITY response code when the mailbox is selected, and if unique identifiers from an earlier session do not persist, the new validity value must be greater than the one used earlier.

A message sequence number is a relative position from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox, ordered by ascending unique identifier. Sequence numbers can be reassigned during a session: when a message is permanently removed, the numbers of the messages after it go down by one, and a new message can take a number another message held earlier.

Flags are named tokens attached to a message. A system flag is predefined by the specification and begins with a backslash: \Seen, \Answered, \Flagged, \Deleted, \Draft and \Recent. The \Recent flag marks a message that has only just arrived, and the client cannot change it. A keyword is defined by the server implementation and does not begin with a backslash. A flag may be permanent, so that later sessions see the change, or session-only.

The remaining attributes are the internal date and time at which the server received the message, the size of the message in RFC 822 format, a parsed envelope, and a parsed body structure. A client can also fetch only part of a message: the RFC 822 header, the RFC 822 body, a MIME body part, or a MIME header.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can be named in two ways. Its unique identifier never changes and is what a client uses to pick up where it left off, while its sequence number is just its position in the folder and shifts when messages are removed.

sections.title: How IMAP Data Is Written
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 uses textual commands and responses. Data takes one of five forms: an atom, a number, a string, a parenthesized list, or NIL. An atom is one or more non-special characters. A number is one or more digit characters. A parenthesized list is a sequence of data items delimited by space and bounded by parentheses, and lists can be nested by using more levels of parentheses; the empty list is written ().

A string comes in two forms. A literal is the general form: a sequence of zero or more octets, including CR and LF, prefixed with an open brace, the number of octets, a close brace and CRLF. When a client sends a literal it must wait for the server's command continuation request before sending the octets and the rest of the command. A quoted string is an alternative: a sequence of zero or more 7-bit characters, excluding CR and LF, with a double quote at each end. The empty string is written either as two double quotes with nothing between them or as {0} followed by CRLF, and even with a count of zero the client must wait for the continuation request. NIL is the special atom that stands for the non-existence of a data item, which is different from an empty string or an empty list.

Binary data is not permitted: a binary string is any string with NUL characters, so implementations must encode binary data into a textual form such as BASE64 before transmitting it. Characters are 7-bit US-ASCII unless otherwise specified, and other character sets are indicated using a CHARSET. Implementations may transmit 8-bit or multi-octet characters in literals, but should do so only when the character set is identified.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything on the wire is text. A piece of data is either a word, a number, a string, a bracketed list, or NIL, which means the value is missing. Strings that contain awkward characters are sent with their length in front of them.

sections.title: The Commands a Client Can Send
sections.content:
Commands are grouped by the state in which they are permitted. CAPABILITY, NOOP and LOGOUT are valid in any state. In the non-authenticated state the client can also use AUTHENTICATE and LOGIN. In the authenticated state it can use SELECT, EXAMINE, CREATE, DELETE, RENAME, SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE, LIST, LSUB, STATUS and APPEND. In the selected state it can use CHECK, CLOSE, EXPUNGE, SEARCH, FETCH, STORE, COPY and UID.

SELECT opens a mailbox for access. Before it returns OK, the server must send the flags defined in the mailbox, the number of messages as an EXISTS response, the number of recent messages as a RECENT response, and the unique identifier validity value. EXAMINE returns the same information but selects the mailbox read-only. Only one mailbox can be selected at a time in a connection, and selecting another one deselects the first. CREATE, DELETE and RENAME act on whole mailboxes, and APPEND adds a message to a mailbox with given flags and date.

FETCH retrieves data about messages. The data items include FLAGS, INTERNALDATE, RFC822.SIZE, ENVELOPE and BODY, and a body section is written as BODY[HEADER], BODY[TEXT] or BODY[1.2] for a nested part. A suffix of the form <0.100> asks for a run of octets starting at a given offset, so a client can read a large message in pieces. STORE sets and clears flags, SEARCH selects messages by criteria such as header fields or dates, COPY copies messages into another mailbox, and UID does the work of FETCH, STORE, SEARCH or COPY while naming messages by unique identifier instead of sequence number.

A client may send a further command before the previous one has finished, as long as doing so cannot make the results ambiguous. If the server detects a possible ambiguity it must run the commands to completion in the order the client gave them. FETCH, STORE and SEARCH may always be followed immediately, because the server is prohibited from sending an EXPUNGE response while one of them is in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: Each command belongs to a stage of the session: logging in, choosing a folder, or working with the messages inside it. FETCH asks for pieces of a message, so a client can download only the header, or one part of a multipart message, or a slice of the text.

sections.title: Sending Passwords Safely
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 transactions, including electronic mail data, are sent in the clear over the network unless privacy protection is negotiated in the AUTHENTICATE command.

The LOGIN command carries the user name and the plaintext password, so using it sends the password in the clear. The AUTHENTICATE command names an authentication mechanism instead. The exchange is a series of server challenges and client answers specific to that mechanism, where a challenge is a continuation request prefixed with + followed by a BASE64 encoded string and an answer is a line holding a BASE64 encoded string. A client that wishes to cancel sends a line with a single asterisk, and the server must then reject the command with a BAD response. AUTHENTICATE may also negotiate an optional protection mechanism for later interactions. If one is negotiated it applies to all subsequent data on the connection: the stream of command and response octets becomes ciphertext, and each buffer of ciphertext is transferred with a four octet length field in network byte order in front of it.

Authentication mechanisms are optional, and protection mechanisms are optional as well, so an authentication mechanism may be implemented without any protection mechanism. A server error message for an AUTHENTICATE command that fails because of invalid credentials SHOULD NOT detail why the credentials are invalid, and a server error message for a failing LOGIN command SHOULD NOT specify that the user name, as opposed to the password, is invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in IMAP4rev1 is encrypted by itself. The LOGIN command sends the password as plain text, while AUTHENTICATE can run a challenge and answer exchange and can agree to protect the rest of the connection.
